summary: Makera Z1 desktop CNC mill: 200 × 200 × 100 mm, 150 W spindle to 13 000 rev/min, quick tool change by hand, optional laser module.

options.summary: Makera Z1 Pro: the Z1 with closed-loop NEMA 17 steppers that detect lost steps; its other numbers are taken as the Z1's.

sources.from: Makera's published specifications for the Z1 (makera.com product and specification pages, retailer specification sheets) and the Carvera community documentation
Makera's published specifications for the Z1 4th-axis module
Makera's collets for this machine: 1/8" (standard), 1/4", 6, 4 and 3 mm (confirmed by the user)
Makera's buying guides (Z1 vs Z1 Pro; Carvera vs Carvera Air) and the UNSW Making Carvera guide

notes: Tools are changed by hand; the control pauses at each change.
An auto tool setter on the bed and a wired probe (auto Z, levelling, area scan); the 3D probe rod finds edges on conductive stock only (Z1 quick start).
The bit collar installer leaves about 12 mm of a 1/8" bit out of the collet by default (Z1 quick start).
The Z1's X and Y drives are open-loop NEMA 17 steppers and known to be marginal: a heavy cut loses steps without warning. Set axis_force_n when it is known.

A hands-on Z1 Pro review (YouTube 9foCNWyPVMM, pre-production unit) cut aluminium with a 6 mm end mill at Makera's stock depths without trouble, but at 1500-2000 mm/min the Y axis skipped about six times (caught by the Pro's closed loop); chips packed around the axis were a likely factor. Keep aluminium feeds conservative and below max_feed.
The same review found 1/8" bits pack their flutes with aluminium chips; a 6 mm bit is stiffer and clears better, and about 20 mm of stick-out needs the 6 mm shank.
The vacuum bed does not hold parts against a 6 mm bit in aluminium, even at conservative feeds: use it for thin sheet and PCBs only; the vice or corner clamps for metal (same review).

A Z1 owner's test in aluminium (YouTube HK6dePReLUw, 6 mm 3-flute, 12 000 rev/min, 1000 mm/min): adaptive at 2.5 mm deep and 1 mm wide ran cleanly; 3 mm deep and 1 mm wide stalled the spindle twice in the same corner (the control halts on a stall), climb milling in one direction; 0.8 mm wide got through. The load estimate puts these at about 65 %, 78 % and 64 % of the spindle: keep the nominal load nearer 65 % so corner engagement has room.

In that test an undersized shank slipped in the collet under load and the cut deepened pass by pass until the spindle overheated (about 80 °C at 33 °C ambient): check the shank fits the collet before heavy cuts.

A Z1 limit test (YouTube 76JUOc0fC4Y, 2026; standard or Pro not said), 6 mm single-flute in 6061 at 12 000 rev/min and 1000 mm/min, 4 mm wide, deepening the cut: clean to 0.6 mm deep, noisy from 0.7, the spindle slowed at 1.0 and stalled at 1.1 mm (about 41 %, 69 % and 75 % of the spindle by the load estimate). 0.6-0.8 mm deep is the advised safe pass for a 6 mm tool. The spindle stops on overload before damage.

Same test: 7075 reached its limit at about 0.6 mm deep with the same tool (0.4-0.6 advised); a 2.5 mm cutter clogged with chips in 6061 slots past 1.8 mm deep and snapped in 7075 at 1.2 mm; small cutters are limited by chip clearing and stiffness, not power. Practical cutting feed is about 1200 mm/min.

Same test: brass with a 3 mm 4-flute stalled at 0.4 mm deep (0.2 advised); no coolant, fan only (sprayed lubricant used on metal); 3.175 mm chamfer bits vibrate in hard metal, use a 6 mm one. A 0.1 mm press-fit allowance was still tight; a 3D finish in 7075 held about ±0.1 mm.
Same test: the control works to two decimal places and runs arcs as line segments (no G2/G3), and the bed's dowel holes are a clearance fit, so re-fixturing repeats only to about their clearance.
